results.claim: Finite-sequence survival with unrotatable dominoes is in NP.
results.proof_sketch: A certificate specifies the locking position of each domino. For a fixed board state, legal translations of the current fixed-orientation domino form a graph with O(WH) vertices, where W and H are the board dimensions. Reachability from the prescribed spawn position to the claimed locking position can therefore be checked by graph search; locking legality, loss, and deterministic row clears are then checked directly. Repeating this for the explicitly listed sequence takes polynomial time. Equivalently, simple movement paths of polynomial length can be included in the certificate.

results.claim: For row-parallel unrotatable dominoes on an odd-width board, there is a computable linear-size upper bound on the number of pieces that can ever survive.
results.proof_sketch: Track each initial row as a token; a clear deletes one token and introduces a new empty token at the top. Tokens otherwise only move vertically. For initial row i, let its maximal intervals of initially empty cells have lengths ℓi,j and define ci=Σj floor(ℓi,j/2). Initial filled cells remain permanent barriers within that token until the whole row clears, so horizontal dominoes placed in the token form matchings inside these intervals. Thus at most ci pieces can ever occupy token i. The token can clear only if every ℓi,j is even. Let q be the number of initial tokens satisfying this condition and C=Σi ci. If W is odd, a newly introduced empty row has one odd interval of length W and can never clear. Hence at most q rows clear, each introducing one new token of capacity floor(W/2). Therefore no play can place more than U=C+q floor(W/2) dominoes. In particular, an input sequence longer than U is immediately a NO-instance. C, q, and U are computable in O(WH) time.

results.claim: On an even-width board, two initially empty top rows suffice for survival of arbitrarily many row-parallel unrotatable dominoes.
results.proof_sketch: Partition the columns into adjacent pairs. For each pair j, let hj be the highest occupied row in either column, taking hj=0 at the floor. Because the top two rows are empty, hj≤H−2. Drop one domino into each pair; it locks at hj+1 and makes the two column tops equal there. Unless a row clears earlier, repeatedly add dominoes to lower pairs until every pair has top height T=maxj(hj+1)≤H−1. Row T is then full and clears. Every placement is reachable by sliding across the untouched empty top row and descending within its selected pair. If a row clears prematurely, restart. After any such clear, the previously empty top row shifts down and a new empty top row appears, so the top two rows are again empty. Iteration gives an infinite strategy without ever occupying the spawn row.

results.claim: The maximum survival length on an initially empty odd-width W×H board is exactly H floor(W/2).
results.proof_sketch: No row can clear: every row begins with even occupancy, each horizontal domino changes its occupancy by two, while a full odd-width row has odd occupancy. Each row contains at most floor(W/2) disjoint horizontal dominoes, proving the upper bound. For attainability, choose a maximum matching of the W-cell row path that contains the spawn pair; every edge of an odd path extends to such a matching. Fill this same matching level by level from the floor upward. On the top level, place pairs outward-to-inward on each side and place the spawn pair last. One column remains empty in every row, so no clear occurs, and exactly H floor(W/2) pieces lock safely. Combined with the previous claim, an empty even-width board of height at least two permits arbitrary survival.

results.claim: The row-capacity bound is not sufficient, and clearing one row does not guarantee indefinite unrotatable-domino survival.
results.proof_sketch: First, consider a 3×3 board whose only filled cell is the center cell of the middle row. Here C=2 and q=0, so the bound gives U=2. Nevertheless, both possible horizontal pairs are blocked from descending through the middle row. The first domino must lock in the top row, where either placement intersects every possible spawn pair; no second domino can spawn. Thus the true maximum is one. Second, on a 3×2 board with only the bottom-right cell initially filled, a domino in the other two bottom cells clears that row. The resulting empty board accepts exactly two further dominoes, so three pieces survive but a fourth cannot. The preceding odd-width bound certifies optimality: initially C=2 and q=1, giving U=3. Hence a one-line-clear strategy used for rotatable dominoes cannot be transferred directly.

final_writeup:
This gives a rigorous partial classification. The full problem is in NP. For the row-parallel fixed orientation, odd board width admits an O(WH)-computable absolute survival bound U, while even width admits an explicit infinite strategy whenever the two top rows are empty. Empty boards are classified exactly for odd width, and empty even-width boards of height at least two always survive.

The remaining difficulty is genuine reachability rather than area: the 3×3 example proves that even the sharp row-token capacity accounting need not be attainable. Thus these invariants do not yet yield a polynomial-time algorithm. Conversely, the NP-hardness of clearing cited in the source does not by itself imply hardness of survival; a surviving play may leave unmatched residual cells. No reduction establishing NP-hardness, and no polynomial algorithm for arbitrary initial boards, is proved here. Therefore the recorded target is not fully resolved.

If the input formalism permits both horizontal and vertical fixed orientations in one sequence, the NP upper bound applies unchanged, while the remaining claims are precisely scoped to the all-horizontal subfamily.
checks_performed: Read only the designated JSON and used no web resources or other repository files.
Implemented an exact finite-state movement search from the fixed spawn pair, including horizontal/downward reachability, locking, and simultaneous deterministic row deletion.
Exhaustively checked every board with two empty top rows for sizes 2×3, 4×3, 4×4, and 6×3 (4, 16, 256, and 64 lower-row configurations respectively); every state survived 30 tested pieces.
For empty odd-width boards W=3,5,7 and H=1,2,3,4, exact search attained H floor(W/2) pieces and rejected one additional piece in every case.
Exact search confirmed that the 3×3 middle-center obstruction survives exactly one piece and that the 3×2 one-clear example survives exactly three.
All computations were run from /tmp without creating or modifying repository files.
